findings: Anteroposterior (AP) projection radiograph encompassing the lower thorax and abdomen

Highly radiopaque metallic foreign body in the shape of a small teaspoon visible in the left upper quadrant, overlying the gastric region, oriented with the bowl superiorly and handle directed inferiorly and slightly medially
The spoon projects over the gastric fundus/body region, consistent with intragastric location
Marked gaseous distension of the stomach producing a large gas bubble in the left upper quadrant surrounding the spoon
Diffuse coarse haustral pattern visible in the large bowel bilaterally, with moderate fecal loading
Lumbar and lower thoracic spine visible with no gross vertebral body collapse or obvious destructive lesion on this projection
Lower ribs partially visualized; no obvious rib fractures identified
No pneumoperitoneum visible on this projection
No obvious pleural effusion in the imaged lung bases
differential: Ingested metallic foreign body (teaspoon) within the stomach — most likely diagnosis given classic spoon morphology and intragastric gas bubble
Intentional or accidental ingestion with the object lodged at the gastroesophageal junction or proximal stomach — cannot fully exclude without lateral projection
Artificially superimposed or phantom image artifact mimicking a foreign body — considered but morphology and density are consistent with a true metallic object
anatomyConcerns: Only a single AP projection is available; a lateral view would help confirm the depth and exact compartment of the foreign body
The field of view is limited superiorly, partially obscuring the lung bases and mediastinum, limiting assessment for aspiration or mediastinal widening
Significant gastric distension may indicate gastric outlet obstruction or aerophagia secondary to the foreign body
Image slightly rotated to the patient's right, which may alter apparent position of midline structures

imageApproval.diagnosticReason: A clearly radiopaque metallic object with unambiguous teaspoon morphology — ovoid bowl superiorly and tapering handle inferiorly — is visible overlying the left upper quadrant gastric gas bubble, consistent with an intragastric foreign body. No equally supported alternative diagnosis exists; the morphology is too specific for any anatomical structure or other foreign body type. The gastric distension is explained by aerophagia around the foreign body. The slightly superior field extension showing lung bases and partial lower ribs is acceptable for an upper abdomen projection. The pelvis and groin are out of frame as required. Skeletal maturity is consistent with an adult aged 19–39: no open physes are visible, vertebral endplates appear fused. The independent differential's concern about lateral projection is valid but does not undermine the primary diagnosis on this projection. Gastric distension is an expected associated finding and not unexplained. Bowel haustral pattern and fecal loading are normal variants requiring no separate diagnosis.
